spirometry.what: A forced breath out into a tube measures how much air the lungs can move and how fast. It is the test that diagnoses and grades asthma and COPD by separating airways that are narrowed (obstruction) from lungs that are stiff or small (restriction). The spirometer records the volume of air exhaled against time, starting from a maximal breath in, and draws two curves from it: volume against time and flow against volume. From these come the volume blown out in the first second (FEV1), the total volume blown out (FVC) and their ratio, each compared with the value predicted for a person of the same age, sex, height and ethnic background. A result is compared with the normal range for that person: many laboratories use the lower limit of normal, while UK COPD guidance uses a fixed post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.7. Spirometry is also repeated after an inhaled bronchodilator to see whether the obstruction reverses, which supports an asthma diagnosis but does not settle it, and it is used to follow a known lung disease over time. The manoeuvre is standardised by the American Thoracic Society and European Respiratory Society, and the test is only as good as the effort and technique that go into it.

measures.meaning: The volume blown out in the first second; reduced when airways are narrowed. It is the main measure used to grade the severity of obstruction and to follow change over time.
Forced vital capacity, the total volume blown out; reduced when lungs are small or stiff, or when air is trapped behind narrowed airways.

In NICE COPD guidance (NG115) a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7, with typical symptoms, confirms airflow obstruction; GOLD uses the same fixed ratio. ERS/ATS 2022 interpretive standards instead use the lower limit of normal (a z-score below -1.645), and many laboratories report it. A low ratio means air leaves the lungs slowly relative to their size; a normal or high ratio with a low FVC suggests restriction.

In UK asthma guidance (BTS/NICE/SIGN NG245) an FEV1 rise of 12% or more and 200 mL or more after a bronchodilator supports asthma; ERS/ATS 2022 uses a rise of more than 10% of the predicted value. A similar response is also seen in some people with COPD, so it is read with the history and other tests. The test is repeated after inhaling a bronchodilator and the change in FEV1 is measured.
The fastest flow, measured at home on a hand-held meter to track asthma control.
The shape of the curve of flow against volume helps distinguish an obstructive pattern from a restrictive one.
